strengths: WildFeedback contributes a useful NLP resource: 20,281 expert-generated preference pairs, plus model-specific variants, derived from naturally occurring conversational feedback. The combination of feedback extraction, response generation, and preference training offers a practical route for reusing interaction logs. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-01/reviews/b02/review-experiment-fox01k5k/call-cf78ed0743914df98a1ca2c75583025c/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The experiments establish useful training effects across three model families and three public benchmarks. For example, Phi-3 trained on WF GPT-4 improves from 24.3% to 34.9% on AlpacaEval’s length-controlled win rate and from 15.4% to 32.4% on Arena-Hard. Improvements on public benchmark prompts provide evidence beyond the proposed checklist evaluator.

Human validation provides meaningful support for feedback extraction. The study covers 50 conversations and over 500 utterances; GPT-4 achieves 83.3% DSAT precision, with agreement approaching the reported human agreement. The separate 200-conversation evaluation study also helps characterize the automatic evaluator’s reliability.

The manuscript provides annotation rubrics, substantial prompt documentation, model identifiers, training hyperparameters, compute estimates, and a dataset link. Separating test conversations and users from training is a valuable safeguard. These details and the demonstrated training utility support a Findings-level contribution.
weaknesses: The evidence supports training utility more strongly than the broader claims of authentic user alignment and reduced model bias. GPT-4 extracts the preferences, generates or filters training responses, and judges outputs using those preferences. Appendix C measures agreement with annotators following the supplied checklists; it does not establish that the summaries faithfully represent users or that checklist evaluation is more accurate than evaluation without checklists. Agreement is moderate: 57.14%, with κ=0.372, versus 63.27% and κ=0.436 between humans. An independent audit against the original feedback and a matched human comparison of evaluation protocols would substantiate the stronger claims.

The experiments do not isolate the contribution of user feedback. WildFeedback and UltraFeedback differ in prompt distribution, conversation length, dataset size, and preference-pair construction. In particular, WF GPT-4 uses original unsatisfactory responses as negatives, whereas UF GPT-4 ranks two newly generated responses. A control using the same WildChat prompts and generation procedure with feedback removed or shuffled would distinguish feedback benefits from domain adaptation and response-generation effects.

The custom test set deliberately selects central preferences within clusters and tasks resembling training tasks. This defines a restricted evaluation population; it does not establish that the selected preferences represent a majority of users. Conclusions about diverse or evolving preferences therefore exceed the tested scope. Coverage is further limited by feedback-based sampling and DSAT recall of 48.4%, despite the useful precision.

Claims of significant and consistent superiority over UltraFeedback need qualification. Table 3 contains exceptions: Qwen-2 WF GPT-4 scores below UF GPT-4 on AlpacaEval LC (39.4 versus 40.6) and MT-Bench (7.60 versus 7.66). Several other differences are small, and no confidence intervals or variation across training seeds are reported. The substantial improvements over initial models are more convincing than universal superiority over the competing training data.

Some reproducibility details remain underspecified, including the embeddings and selection rule used for clustering, the operational definition of user identity, data-generation decoding settings, and the validation criterion used during hyperparameter search. Explicit split identifiers and executable configurations would strengthen reproducibility. Overall, the resource and empirical gains warrant Findings, while the attribution and evaluation limitations constrain the main-conference case.
